title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Framework for Solving Np-Hard Optimization Problems
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical framework that combines classical preprocessing and postprocessing with quantum subroutines (Quantum Annealing and QAOA) to tackle NP-hard optimization problems. It evaluates the approach on TSP, Knapsack, and Job Scheduling, reporting faster runtimes and near-optimal solutions for larger instances while noting limitations from current quantum hardware, noise, and scalability.
methodology_description: The study proposes and evaluates a hybrid quantum-classical framework that combines classical preprocessing, quantum optimization, and classical postprocessing to solve NP-hard combinatorial problems. Classical preprocessing (dynamic programming, greedy heuristics and other problem-specific heuristics) is used to simplify instances and reduce the search space. The reduced problem is then encoded and handed to quantum subroutines — either Quantum Annealing (QA) on a D-Wave 2000Q machine or QAOA executed via Qiskit on a simulated quantum backend — to explore the solution space and produce candidate solutions. Classical postprocessing (examples given include genetic algorithms and standard constraint-refinement heuristics) refines the quantum-generated candidates to meet real-world constraints. Experiments were carried out on benchmark instances of Traveling Salesman Problem (10–50 cities), Knapsack (50–200 items) and Job Scheduling (50–200 jobs with varying machines). Performance was evaluated by solution quality (optimality gap), computational efficiency (run time, resource usage including number of quantum gates), and scalability versus classical baselines (branch-and-bound, dynamic programming, FCFS/SJF heuristics). Implementations used Python for classical code (SciPy, NumPy), Qiskit for QAOA simulation, and D-Wave Ocean SDK for quantum annealing runs.
experimental_setup: QA experiments run on a D-Wave 2000Q quantum annealer; QAOA implemented and executed using Qiskit on a simulated quantum backend. Classical components implemented in Python using SciPy and NumPy. Problem instances varied in size per problem type (TSP: 10–50 cities; Knapsack: 50–200 items; Job Scheduling: 50–200 jobs).

7) Evaluate solutions against classical baselines (branch-and-bound, DP, heuristics) using metrics (optimality gap, runtime).

results_summary: The paper reports design and empirical evaluation of a hybrid quantum-classical framework applied to TSP, Knapsack, and Job Scheduling. Experiments (using D-Wave QA and simulated QAOA) show the hybrid workflow yielded faster wall-clock runtimes than the classical baselines on the tested instances, with reported speedups ranging from about 2x to 3.33x. Solution quality was described as near-optimal: small instances achieved optimal solutions while larger instances showed nonzero optimality gaps (reported up to 8% for larger TSP instances). The authors list quantum resource usage (roughly 150–250 gates) and emphasize the importance of classical preprocessing/postprocessing. They also acknowledge hardware limitations (noise, decoherence, limited qubits) and frame broader scaling and industrial application claims as contingent on future hardware and algorithmic improvements.
performance_claims: TSP runtime: Hybrid — 15s (10 cities), 60s (30 cities), 180s (50 cities); Classical — 30s (10 cities), 180s (30 cities), 600s (50 cities); Reported speedups: 2x, 3x, 3.33x respectively.
Knapsack runtime: Hybrid — 20s (50 items), 60s (100 items); Classical — 45s (50 items), 180s (100 items); Reported speedups: 2.25x (50 items), 3x (100 items).
Job Scheduling runtime: Hybrid — 25s (50 jobs, 5 machines), 90s (100 jobs, 10 machines); Classical — 55s, 300s respectively; Reported speedups: 2.2x and 3.33x.
Optimality gaps reported for hybrid approach: TSP — 0% (10 cities), 5% (30 cities), 8% (50 cities); Knapsack — 2% (50 items), 4% (100 items); Job Scheduling — 3% (50 jobs), 6% (100 jobs).
Quantum resource usage reported: TSP ~150 gates (10 minutes classical time in hybrid run), Knapsack ~200 gates (15 minutes classical time), Job Scheduling ~250 gates (20 minutes classical time).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports empirical runtime speedups for the specific tested instances and a hybrid workflow, but it does not establish a general or robust quantum advantage for NP-hard problems: solution quality was often non-optimal for larger instances, results rely on limited-size experiments (and simulation for QAOA), and the authors acknowledge hardware and scalability limitations. Consequently, claims of practical quantum advantage remain speculative rather than demonstrated.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — A practical pipeline combining classical preprocessing (heuristics/dynamic programming), quantum optimization (D-Wave QA or QAOA simulator), and classical postprocessing (genetic/local search) to tackle NP-hard combinatorial problems.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Reported empirical speedups (hybrid vs classical) on benchmark instances (e.g., TSP: hybrid times 15/60/180s vs classical 30/180/600s) with near-optimal solution quality (optimality gaps 0%, 5%, 8% for increasing TSP sizes).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates end-to-end experiments using real QA hardware (D-Wave 2000Q) and QAOA on a simulated backend, arguing hybrid approaches can deliver benefits even with current NISQ devices when combined with classical reductions.
#limitation:qubit-count — Authors note current quantum hardware qubit limitations constrain problem mappings and require aggressive classical reduction of instance size before quantum processing.
#limitation:noise — Paper acknowledges hardware noise and quality of quantum samples degrade solution quality and limit scalability to larger, real-world instances.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach relies on problem-specific classical preprocessing to map instances into QUBO/Ising forms; this encoding and reduction step is essential but its cost and potential loss of optimality are not fully quantified.

#limitation:simulation-only — QAOA experiments were run on a simulator (Qiskit) rather than on physical gate-model hardware, which limits claims about gate-model QPU performance under realistic noise.

#contradiction:scalability — Although results claim runtime improvements and near-optimality for tested sizes, the paper simultaneously highlights missing algorithmic details (QAOA depth, shots, anneal counts) and hardware constraints that undermine the strength of scaling/generalization claims.
contradictions: The paper claims hybrid approaches yield runtime speedups and near-optimal solutions on larger instances, but also concedes severe hardware limits (qubit count, noise) and omits crucial algorithmic parameters (QAOA depth, shot counts, annealing schedules). This contradiction weakens the asserted general scalability to real-world problem sizes.

QAOA results are reported from a simulator while QA results come from D-Wave hardware; claiming comparable quantum-enabled gains across both paradigms without gate-model hardware experiments creates an inconsistency in support for broader quantum advantage.
